## Proof

**Answer: Yes, it is possible.**

**Construction.** Let $G = \mathrm{SO}(3)$, the group of rotations of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (i.e., the group of $3\times 3$ real orthogonal matrices with determinant $1$). Let $H$ be the subgroup of rotations about the $z$-axis:

$$H = \left\{\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\right\} \cong S^1.$$

**$G$ is infinite and $H$ is a proper subgroup.** $G = \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is an uncountable (infinite) group. $H$ is a $1$-dimensional subgroup of the $3$-dimensional group $G$, so $H$ is proper. For instance, a rotation about the $x$-axis is not in $H$. We have $|H| = 2^{\aleph_0}$.

**Every element of $G$ lies in some conjugate of $H$.** By **Euler's rotation theorem**, every element $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a rotation by some angle $\theta$ about some axis through the origin. That is, there exists a unit vector $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $R$ fixes the line spanned by $\mathbf{v}$ and rotates the orthogonal complement by angle $\theta$.

The conjugates of $H$ in $G$ are precisely the subgroups of rotations about all possible axes through the origin. Indeed, conjugating $H$ (rotations about the $z$-axis) by an element $g \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ that maps the $z$-axis to the axis determined by $\mathbf{v}$ yields the subgroup of all rotations about the axis $\mathbf{v}$.

Since every $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a rotation about some axis $\mathbf{v}$, it follows that $R$ belongs to the subgroup of rotations about $\mathbf{v}$, which is a conjugate of $H$. Therefore:

$$\bigcup_{g \in G} gHg^{-1} = G.$$

**The complement is empty.** The set of elements of $G$ not lying in any conjugate of $H$ is:

$$G \setminus \bigcup_{g \in G} gHg^{-1} = \emptyset,$$

which has cardinality $0$.

**Conclusion.** The number of elements not in any conjugate of $H$ is $0$, while $|H| = 2^{\aleph_0} > 0$. Thus:

$$\left|G \setminus \bigcup_{g \in G} gHg^{-1}\right| = 0 < |H|.$$

This shows that an infinite group can indeed have a proper subgroup such that the number of elements not in any conjugate of that subgroup is less than the order of the subgroup. $\blacksquare$

## Proof

**Answer: Yes, it is possible.**

**Construction.** Let $G = \mathrm{SO}(3)$, the group of rotations of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (i.e., the group of $3\times 3$ real orthogonal matrices with determinant $1$). Let $H$ be the subgroup of rotations about the $z$-axis:

$$H = \left\{\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\right\} \cong S^1.$$

**$G$ is infinite and $H$ is a proper subgroup.** $G = \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is an uncountable (infinite) group. $H$ is a $1$-dimensional subgroup of the $3$-dimensional group $G$, so $H$ is proper. For instance, a rotation about the $x$-axis is not in $H$. We have $|H| = 2^{\aleph_0}$.

**Every element of $G$ lies in some conjugate of $H$.** By **Euler's rotation theorem**, every element $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a rotation by some angle $\theta$ about some axis through the origin. That is, there exists a unit vector $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $R$ fixes the line spanned by $\mathbf{v}$ and rotates the orthogonal complement by angle $\theta$.

The conjugates of $H$ in $G$ are precisely the subgroups of rotations about all possible axes through the origin. Indeed, conjugating $H$ (rotations about the $z$-axis) by an element $g \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ that maps the $z$-axis to the axis determined by $\mathbf{v}$ yields the subgroup of all rotations about the axis $\mathbf{v}$.

Since every $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a rotation about some axis $\mathbf{v}$, it follows that $R$ belongs to the subgroup of rotations about $\mathbf{v}$, which is a conjugate of $H$. Therefore:

$$\bigcup_{g \in G} gHg^{-1} = G.$$

**The complement is empty.** The set of elements of $G$ not lying in any conjugate of $H$ is:

$$G \setminus \bigcup_{g \in G} gHg^{-1} = \emptyset,$$

which has cardinality $0$.

**Conclusion.** The number of elements not in any conjugate of $H$ is $0$, while $|H| = 2^{\aleph_0} > 0$. Thus:

$$\left|G \setminus \bigcup_{g \in G} gHg^{-1}\right| = 0 < |H|.$$

This shows that an infinite group can indeed have a proper subgroup such that the number of elements not in any conjugate of that subgroup is less than the order of the subgroup. $\blacksquare$
